claim: Ovarian cancer is the most devastating gynecological malignancy, with high morbidity and ranking fifth among all cancer-related mortality in women.
source: Ovarian cancer is the most devastating gynecological malignancy, with high morbidity and ranking fifth among all cancer-related mortality in women (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Siegel et al., 2020.

claim: Patients with ovarian carcinoma are usually diagnosed at an advanced stage, resulting in a very low 5-year survival rate.
source: Patients with ovarian carcinoma are usually diagnosed at an advanced stage, resulting in a very low 5-year survival rate (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Siegel et al., 2020.

claim: The lack of a genetically engineered mouse model for ovarian cancer significantly delays the entire process of ovarian cancer research.
source: The lack of a genetically engineered mouse model for ovarian cancer significantly delays the entire process of ovarian cancer research.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of ovarian cancer research models, presented as established knowledge.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of ovarian tumor progression and metastasis are not well understood.
source: In particular, the molecular mechanisms of ovarian tumor progression and metastasis are not well understood, key factors severely restricting the overall survival from ovarian cancer (Binaschi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Binaschi et al., 2011.

claim: FER protein has been shown to be aberrantly upregulated and activated in different types of carcinoma.
source: Notably, the FER protein has been shown to be aberrantly upregulated and activated in different types of carcinoma (Yang et al., 2009; Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Albeck and Brugge, 2011; Ren et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Yang et al., 2009; Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Albeck and Brugge, 2011; Ren et al., 2012.

claim: High activity of FER protein kinase has been observed in 22% of ovarian cancer tumor samples via a global phosphoproteomic approach.
source: Specifically, high activity of FER protein kinase has been observed in 22% of ovarian cancer tumor samples via a global phosphoproteomic approach (Ren et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ren et al., 2012.

claim: STAT3, cortactin, MET, and CRMP2 have been verified as FER substrates.
source: Meanwhile, STAT3, cortactin, MET, and CRMP2, the functions of which are intensively involved in tumor cell motility and chemo-resistance, have been verified as FER substrates (Orlovsky et al., 2002; Fan et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Orlovsky et al., 2002; Fan et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: FER expression has been associated with proliferation of tumor cells.
source: In addition to motility, FER expression has also been associated with proliferation of tumor cells (Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Allard et al., 2000; Lennartsson et al., 2013; Oneyama et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Allard et al., 2000; Lennartsson et al., 2013; Oneyama et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2019.

claim: Significant numbers of proteins could be modified by tyrosine phosphorylation in cells expressing FER-WT compared to FER-K591R.
source: We observed that significant numbers of proteins could be modified by tyrosine phosphorylation in cells expressing FER-WT compared to FER-K591R (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 2298 candidate substrates with scores above 100 were obtained from in-gel tryptic digestion mass spectrometry analysis.
source: We obtained 2298 candidate substrates with scores above 100 (Figure 1B and Supplementary files 1-6).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data referenced in Figure 1B and supplementary files.

claim: 153 candidate proteins were identified from on-bead tryptic digestion followed by mass spectrometry.
source: With this procedure we identified 153 candidate proteins (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data referenced in Figure 1B and supplementary file 7.

claim: 99 overlapped hits were obtained by combining results from two mass spectrometry experiments.
source: Combining results from the two experiments, we obtained 99 overlapped hits for further examination (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FER was identified as its own substrate since the Tyr402 residue of the kinase is known to be auto-phosphorylated.
source: Notably, we identified FER as its own substrate since the Tyr402 residue of the kinase is known to be auto-phosphorylated (Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2016.

claim: IGF1R was identified as a candidate FER substrate.
source: We also identified IGF1R, a key tyrosine kinase receptor in regulating cancer cell survival, proliferation, and motility (Stanicka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to Stanicka et al., 2018 for IGF1R function.

claim: IRS4 binds to FER.
source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, IRS4 binds to FER and this association was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The association between IRS4 and FER was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, IRS4 binds to FER and this association was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The binding of GRB2 to IRS4 was FER kinase activity-dependent.
source: Interestingly, the binding of GRB2 to IRS4 was FER kinase activity-dependent (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER.
source: Surprisingly, the shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER, indicating the N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction with FER.
source: Surprisingly, the shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER, indicating the N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the binding data of truncation mutants shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants of IRS4 demonstrated no binding affinity with FER.
source: Whereas the 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants demonstrated no binding affinity with FER, the 200–400 mutant maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 200–400 mutant of IRS4 maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER.
source: Whereas the 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants demonstrated no binding affinity with FER, the 200–400 mutant maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The N-terminal 1–334aa of IRS4 showed strongest binding among all truncated constructs tested.
source: The N-terminal mutant 1–334 showed strongest binding among all these truncated constructs (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both PH and PTB domains of IRS4 are involved in binding with FER.
source: However, all three mutants showed as strong binding affinity with FER as WT IRS4, suggesting both PH and PTB domains were involved (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Deletion of PH or PTB domain has minimal effect on binding affinity of IRS4 with FER.
source: Interestingly, deletion of PH or PTB domain has minimal effect on binding affinity with FER (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting disrupt either of these domains is not sufficient to collapse the protein complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER showed robust interaction with IRS4.
source: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER, rather than its N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains), showed robust interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains) of FER did not show interaction with IRS4.
source: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER, rather than its N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains), showed robust interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, was involved in interaction with IRS4.
source: Notably, FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, was involved in interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: FER kinase domain showed strong interaction with either PH domain (1–200aa) or PTB domain (200–400aa) of IRS4.
source: Furthermore, FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, showed strong interaction with either PH domain (1–200aa) or PTB domain (200–400aa) of IRS4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Among seven non-receptor tyrosine kinases tested, FER illustrated highest capability for tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, among all these kinases, FER illustrated highest capability for tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IRS4 is a bona fide FER substrate.
source: This result demonstrates that IRS4 is a bona fide FER substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of IRS4 was increased in an FER kinase dosage-dependent manner.
source: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of IRS4 was increased in an FER kinase dosage-dependent manner (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tyrosine residues between 700 and 1093 amino acids of IRS4 were potential substrate(s) for FER kinase.
source: We concluded tyrosine residues between 700 and 1093 amino acids of IRS4 were potential substrate(s) for FER kinase, since: (1) the 1–1093 mutant of IRS4 showed equivalent phosphorylation level to full-length IRS4 upon FER phosphorylation; (2) compared to the 1–699 mutant, 1–800 mutant of IRS4 showed weak but significant amount of phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phosphorylation data of IRS4 truncation mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Three tyrosine sites, Y656, Y828, and Y921, were repeatedly detected as phosphorylated in both mass spectrometry datasets.
source: By performing mass spectrometry analysis in duplicate, we observed three tyrosine sites, namely Y656, Y828, and Y921, whose phosphorylation were repeatedly detected in both datasets (Figure 3D and Supplementary files 8-9).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary files 8-9.

claim: Y847 was detected as phosphorylated once in mass spectrometry analysis.
source: Y847 was also detected once (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary file 8.

claim: A tyrosine to phenylalanine substitution at residue 779 remarkably decreased the phosphorylation level of IRS4 in the presence of FER.
source: Excluding the Y828, Y847, and Y921 mutants, a tyrosine to phenylalanine substitution at residue 779 remarkably decreased the phosphorylation level of IRS4 in the presence of FER (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of 5YF mutant by FER was profoundly diminished compared to each single mutant.
source: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of 5YF mutant by FER was profoundly diminished compared to each single mutant (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There are five major tyrosine residues within IRS4 that are subjected to FER-mediated phosphorylation.
source: These results highly suggest that there are five major tyrosine residues within IRS4 that are subjected to FER-mediated phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mass spectrometry and mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Two ovarian carcinoma-derived cell lines, OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3, showed evident upregulation of IRS4 protein expression compared to normal HOSE control cells.
source: Compared to normal HOSE control cells, two ovarian carcinoma-derived cell lines, OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3, showed evident upregulation of IRS4 protein expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the proliferation capacity of HEY and OVCAR-8 cells.
source: Notably, Cell Titer-Glo (CTG) luminescent cell viability assay demonstrated that the expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the proliferation capacity of these cells (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Loss of IRS4 has minimal effect on OVCAR-5 cell survival.
source: Results from Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) double staining assay indicated that loss of IRS4 has minimal effect on OVCAR-5 cell survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Annexin V-FITC and PI staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of IRS4 significantly decreased the proportion of cells within S phase.
source: Further cell cycle analysis in both WT and IRS4 KO cell lines with PI staining indicated that loss of IRS4 significantly decreased the proportion of cells within S phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The KO of IRS4 notably delayed the proliferation capacity of OVCAR-5 cells.
source: Consistently, CTG assay demonstrated that the KO of IRS4 notably delayed the proliferation capacity of OVCAR-5 cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ectopic re-expression of IRS4, rather than an empty vector, restored the potential of cell proliferation in IRS4-KO ovarian cancer cells.
source: Ectopic re-expression of IRS4, rather than an empty vector, restored the potential of cell proliferation in IRS4-KO ovarian cancer cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Loss of IRS4 in OVCAR-3 cells led to growth retardation.
source: Consistent with KO studies in OVCAR-5 cells, loss of IRS4 in OVCAR-3 cells also led to growth retardation (Figure 4J), highlighting the key role of IRS4 in maintaining ovarian tumor cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Ectopic expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the level of phospho-AKT in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells.
source: Interestingly, ectopic expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the level of phospho-AKT in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: A dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT was observed in both OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells and OVCAR-3 IRS4-KD cells.
source: Consistently, we also observed a dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT in both OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells (Figure 4F) and OVCAR-3 IRS4-KD cells (Figure 4I), indicating a tight correlation between PI3K-AKT pathway and ovarian cancer cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4F and 4I.

claim: The inhibition of the PI3K-AKT pathway in OVCAR-5 cells decreased the phosphorylation level of AKT and cell growth in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: To confirm this, we treated OVCAR-5 WT cells with PI3K inhibitor LY294002 (Figure 4K–L) and demonstrated that the inhibition of the PI3K-AKT pathway in OVCAR-5 cells indeed decreased the phosphorylation level of AKT and cell growth in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4K-L.

claim: 16 out of 30 compounds that showed proliferation inhibition greater than 75% targeted the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway.
source: Thirty out of 198 compounds showed proliferation inhibition greater than 75% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Among these, 16 compounds targeted the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by compound library screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Evident elevation in phospho-ERK level was observed in OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, whereas there was a dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT signal upon IRS4 deletion, we also observed evident elevation in phospho-ERK level in OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells (Figure 4F), indicating a potential compensatory effect of ERK signaling pathway which may contribute to the survival and proliferative capacities of OVCAR-5 cancer cells after IRS4 deletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The inhibition of both PI3K-AKT pathway and ERK pathway in OVCAR-5 cells almost blocked cell growth completely.
source: The inhibition of both PI3K-AKT pathway and ERK pathway in OVCAR-5 cells almost blocked cell growth completely (Figure 4M).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: PIK3R2 preferred to bind with WT rather than the Y779F mutant of IRS4.
source: Notably, we observed that PIK3R2 (the regulatory subunit of PI3K) preferred to bind with WT rather than the Y779F mutant of IRS4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The preferential association of PIK3R2 appeared when comparing interaction proteins between WT and 5YF mutant of IRS4.
source: Interestingly, this preferential association of PIK3R2 appeared again when comparing interaction proteins between WT and 5YF mutant of IRS4 (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2.
source: Compared to the WT control, the Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2, and subsequently decreased AKT phosphorylation as well (Figure 5H), indicating the importance of the tyrosine phosphorylation of the 779 residue (as mediated by FER) in recruiting PIK3R2 and AKT activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The Y779F mutation of IRS4 led to decreased AKT phosphorylation.
source: Compared to the WT control, the Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2, and subsequently decreased AKT phosphorylation as well (Figure 5H), indicating the importance of the tyrosine phosphorylation of the 779 residue (as mediated by FER) in recruiting PIK3R2 and AKT activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4.
source: Further co-immunoprecipitation assay demonstrated that both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4, and the presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex.
source: Further co-immunoprecipitation assay demonstrated that both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4, and the presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PIK3R1 could form complex with both WT and Y779F mutant of IRS4 with equivalent binding affinity.
source: More interestingly, unlike PIK3R2, PIK3R1 could form complex with both WT and Y779F mutant of IRS4 with equivalent binding affinity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Distinctive binding mechanisms were harnessed by PIK3R1 and PIK3R2, respectively, to form complex with IRS4.
source: Therefore, distinctive binding mechanisms were harnessed by PIK3R1 and PIK3R2, respectively, to form complex with IRS4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding patterns of PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 with IRS4 mutants.

claim: OVCAR-5 cell lysates with anti-FER or anti-IRS4 antibody showed robust interaction between FER and IRS4 at endogenous level.
source: Compared to anti-IgG control, the OVCAR-5 cell lysates with anti-FER or anti-IRS4 antibody showed the robust interaction between FER and IRS4 at endogenous level (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The interaction between FER and IRS4 disappeared upon CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KO of either FER or IRS4.
source: Such interaction was disappeared upon CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KO of either FER or IRS4 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Decreased tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 was observed after FER KO in OVCAR-5 cells.
source: We observed decreased tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 after tandem IRS4 immunoprecipitation and pTyr immunoblotting (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The association of IRS4 and PIK3R2 was decreased in FER-deficient OVCAR-5 ovarian cancer cells.
source: The association of IRS4 and PIK3R2 was also decreased in FER-deficient OVCAR-5 ovarian cancer cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 in the presence of ligand IGF1.
source: IGF1R indeed phosphorylated IRS4 in the presence of ligand IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1.
source: However, small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 in an IGF1-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 occurs in an IGF1-independent manner.
source: However, small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 in an IGF1-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that IGF1R inhibition doesn't affect IRS4 phosphorylation in the absence of IGF1.

claim: IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 probably in a Tyr779-independent manner.
source: Moreover, IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 probably in a Tyr779-independent manner, since mutating tyrosine 779 to phenylalanine didn't decrease phosphorylation level of IRS4 mediated by IGF1R receptor tyrosine kinase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Y779F mutation doesn't affect IGF1R-mediated phosphorylation of IRS4.

claim: TAE684 can robustly inhibit the auto-phosphorylation of FER at Tyr402, with IC50 around 8.8 nM.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, TAE684 can robustly inhibit the auto-phosphorylation of FER at Tyr402, with IC50 around 8.8 nM.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and dose-response data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No FES expression was detected in ovarian cancer cell lines used in this study.
source: Interestingly, compared to lysates from myeloid leukemia cell HL-60, we detected no FES expression in ovarian cancer cell lines used in this study (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ovarian cells treated with TAE684 showed dose-dependent inhibition on the kinase activity of FER.
source: Of note, ovarian cells treated with TAE684 did show dose-dependent inhibition on the kinase activity of FER, as illustrated by pY402 FER blotting analysis (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 was observed in the presence of TAE684.
source: Meanwhile, we witnessed the reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4, as well as decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 in the presence of TAE684 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 was observed in the presence of TAE684.
source: Meanwhile, we witnessed the reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4, as well as decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 in the presence of TAE684 (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The kinase activity of AKT was largely dampened upon TAE684 treatment.
source: Of note, the kinase activity of AKT was largely dampened upon TAE684 treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect.
source: Whereas re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect, 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation in IRS4-KO cells.
source: Whereas re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect, 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cells re-expressing the Y779F mutant of IRS4 showed significantly delayed proliferation rate compared to the parental ovarian cancer cells.
source: We did observe a certain extent of growth defect rescue with cells re-expressing in the Y779F mutant of IRS4, but these cells still showed significantly delayed proliferation rate compared to the parental ovarian cancer cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone.
source: Consistently, IRS4 KO OVCAR-5 cells treated with U0126 demonstrated profound inhibition in cell growth (Figure 6F). Most importantly, re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone, whereas 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment.
source: Most importantly, re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone, whereas 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: OVCAR-5 cells treated with TAE684 showed a dose-dependent growth inhibition.
source: In addition, OVCAR-5 cells treated with TAE684 showed a dose-dependent growth inhibition, as illustrated by CTG assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Significantly delayed tumor formation was observed in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells with an empty vector compared to mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with WT IRS4.
source: Compared to mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with WT IRS4, we observed significantly delayed tumor formation in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells with an empty vector (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Tumor growth in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with 5YF IRS4 was profoundly delayed compared to WT control.
source: Consistent with our previous findings in cell cultures, the tumor growth in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with 5YF IRS4 was profoundly delayed compared to WT control (Figure 6G), further emphasizing the necessity of the tyrosine phosphorylation of key residues in IRS4 for ovarian tumorigenesis and progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Ectopic expression of IRS4 in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells significantly accelerated tumor formations compared to parental controls.
source: Consistently, ectopic expression of IRS4 in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells significantly accelerated tumor formations compared to parental controls (Figure 6H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6H-K.

claim: IRS4 shows the highest mRNA transcript abundance in the ovaries, followed by the thyroid gland and endometrium.
source: Interestingly, IRS4 shows the highest mRNA transcript abundance in the ovaries, followed by the thyroid gland and endometrium (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas dataset shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A higher expression of IRS4 was observed in ovarian cancer patient samples compared to normal ovaries.
source: In line with our findings in cell cultures, we observed a higher expression of IRS4 in ovarian cancer patient samples (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue microarray data from the Human Protein Atlas database shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The expression levels of IRS4 in ovarian tumor samples were significantly elevated compared to normal control samples.
source: In accordance with the result from HPA database, the expression levels of IRS4 in ovarian tumor samples were significantly elevated compared to normal control samples (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry staining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A lower expression of IRS4 was correlated to longer overall survival in patients with ovarian cancer.
source: The result demonstrated that a lower expression of IRS4 was correlated to longer overall survival in patients with ovarian cancer (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data analysis from over 600 ovarian cancer patients shown in Figure 7E.

claim: IRS4 was significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancers.
source: In conclusion, IRS4 was significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancers and its upregulation was inversely correlated with survival and prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunoblotting, immunohistochemistry, and clinical data analysis.

claim: Upregulation of IRS4 was inversely correlated with survival and prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.
source: In conclusion, IRS4 was significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancers and its upregulation was inversely correlated with survival and prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: IRS4 has no SHP2 binding motif to recruit tyrosine phosphatase SHP2.
source: Unlike IRS1 and IRS2, IRS4 has no SHP2 binding motif to recruit tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (Wauman et al., 2008; Fantin et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wauman et al., 2008 and Fantin et al., 1998.

claim: The unique feature of IRS4 lacking SHP2 binding motif allows IRS4 to maintain constitutive hyperactivation of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway.
source: This unique feature allows IRS4 to maintain constitutive hyperactivation of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway (Wauman et al., 2008; Fantin et al., 1998; Cuevas et al., 2007), leading to growth factor-independent cell proliferation and tumorigenesis in mammary epithelial cells (Ikink et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wauman et al., 2008; Fantin et al., 1998; Cuevas et al., 2007; and Ikink et al., 2016.

claim: FER binds directly to IRS4 and phosphorylates several tyrosine residues on IRS4.
source: Combining mass spectrometry analysis with biochemical and biological approaches, we have revealed one of the IRS family members, IRS4, as a novel substrate of non-receptor tyrosine kinase FER. FER binds directly to IRS4 (Figure 2) and phosphorylates several tyrosine residues on IRS4 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 on IRS4 is critical in recruiting PIK3R2/p85β.
source: The proximity labeling PUP-IT assay further confirmed that FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 on IRS4 is critical in recruiting PIK3R2/p85β, the key regulatory subunit of PI3K kinase (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ectopic overexpression of FER dramatically increased tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4.
source: While ectopic overexpression of FER dramatically increased tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4, CRISPR-Cas9 directed KO or pharmacological inhibition of the endogenous kinase in ovarian cancer cells remarkably reduced tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from overexpression studies.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 directed KO or pharmacological inhibition of the endogenous FER kinase in ovarian cancer cells remarkably reduced tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4.
source: While ectopic overexpression of FER dramatically increased tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4, CRISPR-Cas9 directed KO or pharmacological inhibition of the endogenous kinase in ovarian cancer cells remarkably reduced tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment of IRS4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from knockout and inhibitor studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: In IRS4-positive ovarian cancer cells, FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 enables IRS4 to recruit PIK3R2/p85β and activate the PI3K-AKT pathway for proliferation.
source: We think this key difference could explain the different functional output of FER in both experimental context: In the absence of IRS4, FER regulates ovarian cancer cell motility and invasiveness mainly through MET-GAB1-SHP2-ERK1/2 signaling pathway, with MET and GAB1 as its substrates; in IRS4-positive ovarian cancer cells, FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 enables IRS4 to recruit PIK3R2/p85β, the regulatory subunit of PI3K, and activate the PI3K-AKT pathway for proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of FER function in different cellular contexts.

claim: In the absence of IRS4, FER regulates ovarian cancer cell motility and invasiveness mainly through MET-GAB1-SHP2-ERK1/2 signaling pathway.
source: We think this key difference could explain the different functional output of FER in both experimental context: In the absence of IRS4, FER regulates ovarian cancer cell motility and invasiveness mainly through MET-GAB1-SHP2-ERK1/2 signaling pathway, with MET and GAB1 as its substrates; in IRS4-positive ovarian cancer cells, FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 enables IRS4 to recruit PIK3R2/p85β, the regulatory subunit of PI3K, and activate the PI3K-AKT pathway for proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of FER function in different cellular contexts and supported by previous work.

claim: FER is upregulated in both OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3 cell lines.
source: Of note, FER is also upregulated in both cell lines (Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2016.

claim: The binding between FER and IRS4 was not affected in the absence and/or presence of IRS1.
source: Notably, the binding between FER and IRS4 was not affected in the absence and/or presence of IRS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Interaction between IRS1 and FER has been demonstrated in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Masanori Iwanishi and his colleagues have demonstrated interaction between IRS1 and FER in 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Iwanishi et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Iwanishi et al., 2000.

claim: The 1–550aa truncation mutant of IRS4 possessed weak but detectable phosphorylation signals in the presence of FER kinase.
source: However, it also should not be ignored that the 1–550aa truncation mutant of IRS4 also possessed weak but detectable phosphorylation signals in the presence of FER kinase.
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphorylation data of IRS4 truncation mutants.

claim: Tyr487 of human IRS4 resembles YXXM motif that upon phosphorylation is predicted to bind SH2 domains in the p85 regulatory subunit of PI3K.
source: Actually, Tyr487 of human IRS4 also resembles YXXM motif that upon phosphorylation is predicted to bind SH2 domains in the p85 regulatory subunit of PI3K.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge of YXXM motifs.

claim: Among five major Tyr residues, Tyr779, -828, and -921 reside in YXXM motifs to create potential PI3K binding sites.
source: Among five major Tyr residues, Tyr779, -828, and -921 reside in YXXM motifs to create potential PI3K binding sites.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of IRS4.

claim: FER is significantly upregulated in ovarian cancer cell lines and ovarian cancer tumor samples, compared to normal controls.
source: It has been reported that FER is significantly upregulated in ovarian cancer cell lines and ovarian cancer tumor samples, compared to normal controls and that its downregulation by RNAi results in substantial attenuation of tumor cell migration, invasion, and metastasis, with little change in primary tumor growth (Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2016.

claim: Downregulation of FER by RNAi results in substantial attenuation of tumor cell migration, invasion, and metastasis, with little change in primary tumor growth.
source: It has been reported that FER is significantly upregulated in ovarian cancer cell lines and ovarian cancer tumor samples, compared to normal controls and that its downregulation by RNAi results in substantial attenuation of tumor cell migration, invasion, and metastasis, with little change in primary tumor growth (Fan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2016.

claim: CAOV4 cells express no IRS4.
source: In the previous report, CAOV4 cells have been used in the majority of in vivo assays, which expresses no IRS4.
evidence: The claim is based on characterization of cell lines used in previous studies.

claim: OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3 have high IRS4 expression.
source: However, two cell lines used in this study, OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3, have high IRS4 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TAE684 has been identified as a potent inhibitor against FES.
source: In a screen of 586 compounds, TAE684 has been identified as a potent inhibitor against FES, the family member of FER (Hellwig et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hellwig et al., 2012.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation has been reported as an important layer of regulation for transporter proteins' stability.
source: Notably, tyrosine phosphorylation has been reported as an important layer of regulation for transporter proteins' stability (Loureiro et al., 2019) and activity (Xu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2016; Hedges et al., 2013; Wertheimer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loureiro et al., 2019.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation has been reported as an important layer of regulation for transporter proteins' activity.
source: Notably, tyrosine phosphorylation has been reported as an important layer of regulation for transporter proteins' stability (Loureiro et al., 2019) and activity (Xu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2016; Hedges et al., 2013; Wertheimer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2016; Hedges et al., 2013; Wertheimer et al., 2008.

claim: FER directly phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate 4 (IRS4).
source: By integrating mass spectrometry analysis with biochemical and biological approaches, we have demonstrated that FER directly phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate 4 (IRS4) and that this tyrosine phosphorylation is important to create a binding site for recruiting PIK3R2/p85β.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including mass spectrometry and in vitro kinase assays.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 by FER is important to create a binding site for recruiting PIK3R2/p85β.
source: By integrating mass spectrometry analysis with biochemical and biological approaches, we have demonstrated that FER directly phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate 4 (IRS4) and that this tyrosine phosphorylation is important to create a binding site for recruiting PIK3R2/p85β.
evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Recruitment of PIK3R2/p85β onto IRS4 is required for PI3K-AKT signaling pathway activation and tumorigenesis in ovarian cancer.
source: As the key regulatory subunit of PI3K kinase, recruitment of PIK3R2/p85β onto IRS4 is required for PI3K-AKT signaling pathway activation and tumorigenesis in ovarian cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including cell proliferation assays and xenograft studies.

claim: Rescuing IRS4-null ovarian tumor cells with phosphorylation-defective mutant delayed ovarian tumor cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Rescuing IRS4-null ovarian tumor cells with phosphorylation-defective mutant, but not WT IRS4 delayed ovarian tumor cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assays and xenograft tumor growth data.

claim: Rescuing IRS4-null ovarian tumor cells with WT IRS4 did not delay ovarian tumor cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Rescuing IRS4-null ovarian tumor cells with phosphorylation-defective mutant, but not WT IRS4 delayed ovarian tumor cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell proliferation assays and xenograft tumor growth data.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of FER kinase may be beneficial for ovarian cancer patients with PI3K-AKT hyperactivation.
source: Overall, we revealed a kinase-substrate mode between FER and IRS4, and the pharmacological inhibition of FER kinase may be beneficial for ovarian cancer patients with PI3K-AKT hyperactivation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings of the study regarding FER's role in PI3K-AKT activation.

claim: FER engaged its kinase domain to associate with the PH and PTB domains of IRS4.
source: FER engaged its kinase domain to associate with the PH and PTB domains of IRS4.
evidence: The claim is supported by domain mapping experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 enables IRS4 to recruit PIK3R2/p85β and activate the PI3K-AKT pathway.
source: Using a proximity-based tagging system in ovarian carcinoma-derived OVCAR-5 cells, we determined that FER-mediated phosphorylation of Tyr779 enables IRS4 to recruit PIK3R2/p85β, the regulatory subunit of PI3K, and activate the PI3K-AKT pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assays and biochemical experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Non-receptor tyrosine kinase FER is upregulated in ovarian cancer.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated that non-receptor tyrosine kinase FER is upregulated in ovarian cancer, knocking down which attenuates metastatic phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Knocking down FER attenuates metastatic phenotypes in ovarian cancer.
source: Our previous work has demonstrated that non-receptor tyrosine kinase FER is upregulated in ovarian cancer, knocking down which attenuates metastatic phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous work from the authors' lab.
